subject: social_sciences
chapter_title: Chapter 10: A Journey Through Indian Architecture

competencies.justification: C-7.1 names art among the cultural elements through which India's unity in diversity is to be explained, and that explanation is the chapter's fundamental organising purpose. Its architecture is a survey of diverse traditions — 'The Beginnings …' on Harappan urban planning, 'Structural Stupa Architecture', 'Rock-Cut Architecture' spanning Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves, 'Water Structures' differing by region from the Thar to the Northeast, 'Classical Temple Architecture' comparing Thanjavur, Bhubaneswar, Mount Abu and Bishnupur, 'The Architecture of Mosques', 'Forts and Palaces', 'Tombs and Mausoleums', 'Traditional Houses' contrasting Shekhawati havelis with Chettinadu houses, 'Churches in India' and 'Colonial Architecture'. Crucially, the chapter's recurring analytic claim across these sections is commonality within that diversity: Ahmedabad's Jama Masjid blends Hindu and Islamic elements with temple-style pillars carved by local Hindu and Jain artisans; Indo-Islamic architecture is defined as exactly such a blend with Rajasthani jharokhas and chhatris; the Taj Mahal is presented as a confluence of Persian, Arabic and Indian traditions; Orchha blends Rajput and Mughal styles; Kerala churches borrow the temple stambha and the sloped tiled roof; and Indo-Saracenic architecture fuses Islamic, Hindu and Gothic elements. Big Question 1 asks what role architecture has played in the Indian civilisation, and removing this competency would dissolve the chapter.

Rule 5(b) is satisfied: the continued prevalence of practices notwithstanding major change is developed deliberately across multiple named sections, and the chapter's own organising logic — a timeline running from Dholavira around 2600 BCE to twentieth-century Mysuru Palace — makes that continuity its explicit frame. 'Rock-Cut Architecture' records that monks circumambulated the stupa at Ellora in the custom of pradakshina and states that the practice persists in later classical temples. 'Traditional Houses' records that the central-courtyard design common in traditional houses was already used in some larger Harappan houses about 4,500 years ago. 'Water Structures' traces an unbroken tradition from Harappan reservoirs and interlocking trapezoid-brick wells through Shringaverpur to the stepwells and temple pushkarinis still used for water harvesting and water-based rituals. 'Classical Temple Architecture' presents temples as continuing centres of cultural life built on the enduring principles of shilpashastra. 'Churches in India' shows a comparatively recent tradition absorbing older local forms. The chapter repeatedly asks the student to recognise the older practice surviving inside the later structure.

Rule 5(b) is satisfied, and C-10.1's demand that the contribution be explained 'in an integrated manner along with the particular matter' is met literally rather than by assertion. 'The Beginnings …' presents Harappan architecture as the earliest known tradition of urban planning and construction in the subcontinent and explains the technical reasoning behind it — brick because of alluvial clay, streets oriented to the cardinal directions, an efficient drain network, and at Dholavira precisely finished stone. 'Water Structures' explains the trapezoid-shaped bricks that lock together so a well shaft cannot collapse inward under infiltration pressure. 'Rock-Cut Architecture' explains the technology by which many thousands of tonnes of rock were removed to leave the monolithic Kailasha Temple. 'Classical Temple Architecture' closes with an explicit integrated comparison, noting that such temples required highly skilled architects, engineers and craftsmen using elaborate techniques and a good deal of mathematics, especially advanced geometry, as was true of Egypt's pyramids, Athens' Parthenon and medieval Europe's Gothic cathedrals, and it presents shilpashastra as a formal discipline. 'Forts and Palaces' explains the Persian wheels that lifted Yamuna water into overhead tanks to feed fountains acting as eco-friendly cooling.

Rule 6 is satisfied and Rule 5 is not. The Introduction names two designated illustrations that guide the whole journey and must be read as data — a map showing where the chosen structures are located, and a timeline placing them in the river of time from Dholavira around 2600 BCE to twentieth-century Mysuru Palace. 'Forts and Palaces' carries a 'Let's Remember' box requiring students to recall the forts of Jaisalmer, Kumbhalgarh, Raigad and Sindhudurg and locate them on that map. Diagrams elsewhere require interpretation rather than viewing: the plan of a densely inhabited area of Mohenjo-daro with its street grid and drains, the plan of a large Harappan house from which the section infers that servants lived downstairs and owners upstairs, and the vertical scheme of the classical temple read as the body of Purusha from shikhara to platform. These are framing and supporting devices distributed through the chapter rather than a dedicated section or an architecturally distinct activity block.

Rule 6 is satisfied. 'Classical Temple Architecture' contains a designated passage whose primary subject is the temple as a social institution and its influence on society — Buddhist, Jain and Hindu places of worship that were also centres of learning, literature, art, social intercourse and economic life, built through royal patronage and donors' endowments. 'The Architecture of Mosques' opens by presenting mosques not only as places of prayer but as centres for religious education, community gatherings, lectures and discussions, with the Friday congregation giving the Jama Masjid its name and Delhi's courtyard holding up to 25,000 people. 'Forts and Palaces' explains forts as institutions housing the residences of ruling and military classes and sometimes an entire city, with Mehrangarh's palace organised into royal areas, separate men's and women's quarters, staff quarters, stables and barracks. 'Rock-Cut Architecture' notes Sharada Peetha as a centre of learning that gave Kashmir the name Sharada Desh, and Bharhut's railing inscriptions record the donors who sustained these institutions.
